Friedrich Nietzsche. A German philosopher from 1844 to 1900 whose radical critique of Western morality, reason, and religion fundamentally reshaped modern thought across philosophy, literature, psychology, and politics. He diagnosed a crisis of meaning he called nihilism and proposed that culture must be remade through the creation of new values. His aphoristic style, psychological insight, and provocative persona made him as influential in twentieth-century art and literature as in academic philosophy.

Nietzsche declared "God is dead." This was not atheist celebration but a diagnosis of modernity's loss of meaning and the collapse of inherited values. He developed the concept of the will to power, arguing that all life seeks not merely survival but dominance, creation, and the overcoming of limits. He critiqued traditional morality—especially Christian and Kantian ethics—as a slave revolt against life, designed by the weak to constrain the strong.

He proposed the Übermensch, often mistranslated as superman or overman. This is not a master race but an ideal figure who creates new values and transcends herd morality. Nietzsche wrote in fragmented, poetic aphorisms rather than systematic treatises, deliberately resisting academic convention. His works Beyond Good and Evil and On the Genealogy of Morals expose the hidden interests and origins behind supposedly universal ethical systems. He introduced perspectivism: there are no absolute truths, only interpretations shaped by the interpreter's values, health, and power.

Nietzsche championed the revaluation of all values. Western culture must overcome Christian slave morality and create life-affirming values rooted in vitality and creativity. He diagnosed decadence in European culture and sought cultural renewal through the recovery of Dionysian impulses—creative, destructive, and ecstatic—alongside Apollonian order. He profoundly influenced modernist artists, psychoanalysts, and existentialists. Tragically, his philosophy was distorted by Nazi ideology, with his sister's editorial interventions complicit in that misuse.
